newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Gov to preserve Medicaid for legal immigrants.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Gov to preserve Medicaid for legal immigrants.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki plans to ensure legal aliens in the state can keep Medicaid benefits under a preliminary welfare plan which will be filed with the U.S. Government tomorrow, a spokesman said on Tuesday.

A spokeswoman for New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who has sued the federal government over new provisions on welfare and immigration, saluted Pataki for his leadership, but suggested the governor's efforts fell short.

"The mayor is still dedicated to serious reversals with the welfare bill," said Christine Lategono, the mayor's director of communications. The city also wants to protect the about 400,000 illegal immigrants who live in New York City.

The Pataki Administration, which has been blasted for risking the loss of millions of dollars a day by not promptly filing at least a preliminary welfare plan with Washington, said that no money had been lost.
"We believe by filing tomorrow that we'll be eligible for the full block grant of $2.4 billion," said John Signor, a spokesman for the state Division of Budget.

Starting October 1, states were allowed to start submitting their plans, which commit them to matching or seeking waivers from the sweeping federal welfare reforms that were signed into law in August.

Signor said New York State's preliminary plan is expected to follow the outlines of one submitted last week by California. California faces some of the same problems as New York, as both have complex, costly systems, and match federal laws with their own.
While New York's plan will set out few of the specific changes the governor plans, Signor said the state does expect to opt out of the new federal rules that limit Medicaid for legal immigrants.

"One of the things we are going to do in the plan is opt out of that so we do continue to provide Medicaid benefits to legal aliens who were covered on August 22, which is when the bill became law," Signor said.

In the next four years, the New York City has estimated that it could lose from $100 million to as much as $600 million if it has to reimburse the federal government and state for the cost of services like Medicaid, public hospital and schools that are used by illegal immigrants.
Precisely how much the city might lose cannot yet be determined, in part because it is not clear how strictly the federal government would apply any penalities, she explained.

The New York City Council has said that up to 245,000 legal residents could lose their benefits in 1998, costing the city up to $370 million. While the Clinton Administration has promised to soften some of these rules, as they now stand 18,500 legal immigrants would lose Medicaid, the council said.
Pataki, who like the mayor is a Republican, soon plans to send the state legislature a detailed bill that will outline what he wants to do with the state's welfare program.
Signor said Pataki still is aiming to call the legislature back for a special session in December to approve a new welfare bill.

Pataki's efforts to reform the state welfare system last spring were blocked by the Assembly, which is controlled by Democrats, but the new federal law includes some of the changes, like time limits, that Pataki had sought.
